title: Jeremiah 29:15–23
context: The same letter continues, answering those among the captives who have said that the LORD has raised them up prophets in Babylon. The LORD speaks concerning the king who sits on David’s throne and concerning the people who still dwell in Jerusalem, the brothers who have not gone into captivity: he will send sword, famine, and pestilence, and will make them like rotten figs that cannot be eaten, tossed among the kingdoms, a horror and a reproach, because they have not listened to the words he sent by his servants the prophets. The captives themselves are told to hear the LORD’s word. Concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who prophesy a lie in the LORD’s name, he will deliver them into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand, and that king will kill them before the captives’ eyes; a curse will be taken up in Babylon, that the LORD would make someone like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire, because they have done foolish things, committed adultery with their neighbors’ wives, and spoken false words in the LORD’s name, which he did not command. The LORD is the one who knows, and is witness. This Zedekiah is not the king in Jerusalem; the two names should not be confused. The adultery and the execution should be told soberly, without graphic expansion. The charge against these two is the letter’s own: a lie in the LORD’s name, with the further sins the verse names. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named by reference as shared ground, without inventing a new true-versus-false-prophet contrast. The king still in Jerusalem and the rotten figs may be compared, without harmonizing, with the fall told in 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52, and with the figs of Jeremiah 24.

verses.text: Because you have said, “The LORD has raised us up prophets in Babylon,”
verses.arminianNotes:
Because they have said, “The LORD has raised us up prophets in Babylon,” the captives’ own saying is taken up: they claim the LORD has raised prophets for them in the land of exile. The letter now answers that claim. The saying may express trust in the very voices verses 8–9 have already warned against, though the text does not name those prophets here.

Arminian readers hear a real boast or comfort the exiles have spoken, which the LORD now takes up, a claim they can be called to measure against the letter itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the quoted words as the occasion of the next judgment: the people have said that the LORD has raised them prophets in Babylon, and he will speak to that claim.

Shared ground: the sentence is their word, not Jeremiah’s invention. What follows concerns both those left in Jerusalem and certain named prophets in Babylon.

verses.text: the LORD says concerning the king who sits on David’s throne, and concerning all the people who dwell in this city, your brothers who haven’t gone with you into captivity,
verses.arminianNotes:
“the LORD says concerning the king who sits on David’s throne, and concerning all the people who dwell in this city, your brothers who haven’t gone with you into captivity,” The first answer looks back to Jerusalem: the king on David’s throne and the people still in the city, brothers who have not gone into captivity. The king is not named here; many readers take him as Zedekiah, a common identification that may be left hedged. 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 tell of that remaining court’s end, and should be named without being blended into this line.

Arminian readers hear a word about those left behind, spoken to the captives so that they will not envy or trust a Jerusalem that the LORD is about to describe as under judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same heading as the LORD’s word about the remaining king and city, the brothers not carried away, whose future the next verses will announce.

Shared ground: the subject is Jerusalem’s remaining court and people. Their identification and dates may be stated modestly.

verses.text: the LORD of Armies says: “Behold, I will send on them the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, and will make them like rotten figs that can’t be eaten, they are so bad.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD of Armies says, “Behold, I will send on them the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, and will make them like rotten figs that can’t be eaten, they are so bad.” The three blows already familiar in these chapters fall on those left in the city, and they are compared to rotten figs too bad to eat. Jeremiah 24 also speaks of figs after a carrying-away; that chapter may be named by reference without being merged with this image.

Arminian readers take the rotten-fig picture as a hard warning about those still in Jerusalem, meant to correct any hope that the ones left behind are the safer or more favored remnant.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same sentence as the LORD’s judgment: sword, famine, pestilence, and a comparison to rotten, uneatable figs.

Shared ground: the remaining city is under this word, not under a promise of quick peace. The fig image should be left as the verse states it.

verses.text: I will pursue after them with the sword, with the famine, and with the pestilence, and will deliver them to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth, to be an object of horror, an astonishment, a hissing, and a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them,
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will pursue after them with the sword, with the famine, and with the pestilence, and will deliver them to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth, to be an object of horror, an astonishment, a hissing, and a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them,” Pursuit and scattering follow. The remaining people will be tossed among kingdoms and become a horror and a reproach in the nations where the LORD has driven them. The sentence runs on into the reason given in the next verse.

Arminian readers hear a real future of scattering held up before the captives, a reason not to trust the safety of those still at home, and a moral seriousness in the driving the LORD names as his own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the pursuit, the tossing among kingdoms, and the horror among the nations as the LORD’s announced work against those left in the city.

Shared ground: the end described is exile and reproach, not deliverance in place. The verse should be read as continuing the word of verse 17.

verses.text: because they have not listened to my words,” says the LORD, “with which I sent to them my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them; but you would not hear,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The reason is “because they have not listened to my words,” says the LORD, “with which I sent to them my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them; but you would not hear,” The remaining city’s judgment is tied to not listening, though the LORD sent his servants the prophets early and often. The phrase “you would not hear” turns the charge toward the hearers of the letter as well, or toward the same stubbornness in both places; a single addressee is not forced beyond what the shift in person allows.

Arminian readers take the unheard sending as a real, repeated appeal that was refused. The prophets were sent, and the not hearing is the people’s own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same ground: the LORD sent his servants the prophets, rising early and sending them, and they would not hear, so the sword and the scattering follow.

Shared ground: judgment is explained by refused words. There is no party contrast over the reason this verse gives.

verses.text: Hear therefore the LORD’s word, all you captives whom I have sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Hear therefore the LORD’s word, all you captives whom I have sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon.” The captives are addressed again, as those the LORD has sent away. They are to hear, not only to watch what befalls Jerusalem.

Arminian readers take the summons as a real call to the exiles themselves. Being already in Babylon does not excuse them from hearing; the letter still claims their attention.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same “Hear therefore” as the LORD’s word to all the captives he has sent away, the audience of what he will now say about two prophets among them.

Shared ground: the captives are the hearers. The next verses name men in their midst, not only the court back in Jerusalem.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and concerning Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who prophesy a lie to you in my name: “Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and he will kill them before your eyes.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD of Armies says concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and concerning Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, “who prophesy a lie to you in my name,” that he will deliver them into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand, “and he will kill them before your eyes.” Two prophets among the captives are named, with their fathers, and are charged with a lie in the LORD’s name. This Zedekiah is the son of Maaseiah, not the king in Jerusalem; the names must be kept distinct. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named by reference as shared ground, without a new contrast. The execution is stated plainly and should not be dwelt on.

Arminian readers take the naming as a specific, public warning the captives can verify in time, a lie in the LORD’s name that will end before their eyes, not a vague slur on unnamed preachers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same verdict: Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah prophesy a lie in the LORD’s name, and they will be delivered to Nebuchadnezzar, who will kill them in the captives’ sight.

Shared ground: the charge is a lie in the LORD’s name, and the outcome is announced. Identities beyond the fathers’ names should not be invented.

verses.text: A curse will be taken up about them by all the captives of Judah who are in Babylon, saying, ‘The LORD make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire;’
verses.arminianNotes:
“A curse will be taken up about them by all the captives of Judah who are in Babylon, saying, ‘The LORD make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire;’” Their death becomes a byword among the captives. The manner of death is the verse’s own word and should be reported soberly, without added description.

Arminian readers hear a grim public memory the exiles themselves will use, a warning that false prophecy in the LORD’s name is not a small offense among them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the curse as the book’s record of how the captives will speak of these two, after the king of Babylon has roasted them in the fire.

Shared ground: the names become a formula of curse in Babylon. The verse is report, not an invitation to linger on the fire.

verses.text: because they have done foolish things in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbors’ wives, and have spoken words in my name falsely, which I didn’t command them. I am he who knows, and am witness,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The reason is “because they have done foolish things in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbors’ wives, and have spoken words in my name falsely, which I didn’t command them.” Then comes the word, “I am he who knows, and am witness,” says the LORD. Beside the false words, foolish acts and adultery are named. Those charges should be kept brief and sober. The LORD knows and is witness; classical Arminians affirm that this knowledge is real and complete, not an open or uncertain watch.

Arminian readers take the three charges as real guilt, including speech the LORD did not command, and the closing words as his own witness, which the people can trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same grounds: foolish things, adultery, and false words in the LORD’s name, which he did not command, and his own claim to know and to be witness.

Shared ground: the LORD knows and testifies. The verse does not require a new contrast over knowledge or over prophecy; the charges are already stated.
